newsitem.title: BELARUS: Tension rises in Belarus after PM offers to quit.
newsitem.headline: Tension rises in Belarus after PM offers to quit.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, branded a dictator by a growing political opposition in the former Soviet republic of Belarus, faced mutiny in his usually loyal government on Monday.
Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir met parliamentary leaders who quoted him as saying he would resign unless Lukashenko cancelled a referendum set for Sunday which would significantly boost his powers.

About 1,000 Belarussians rallied outside parliament, calling on deputies to impeach President Alexander Lukashenko, who is facing growing opposition as he tries to tighten his grip on the former Soviet republic.
"Impeachment! Impeachment!" members of the crowd chanted as 100 deputies met in an emergency session, enough to form a quorum but not enough to impeach the president.
Police barred the entrance to parliament and busloads of other forces kept a watchful eye on the protest, staged by deputies and Lukashenko's communist and nationalist opponents.
A similar protest outside parliament ended in clashes with police on Sunday. Organisers said 20 people were injured and 10 arrested. Police said four officers were also injured.
President Lukashenko, visiting Gomel, near the Ukrainian border, blasted the prime minister on Monday, saying his threat to quit cast doubt on his integrity.
"Nobody is irreplacable," he told a crowd of about 5,000 people, Reuters correspondent Rostislav Khotin reported.
"It's hard to find a milkmaid to milk the cows on a collective farm, but it's never hard to find a bureaucrat -- even if the bureaucrat is prime minister," he said.

Chigir's resignation threat was revealed in Minsk by deputy parliamentary speaker Gennady Karpenko. "Chigir has set the president economic and political conditions, including cancelling the referendum," Karpenko told reporters.
A government official who asked not to be named said Chigir had resigned days ago. Chigir neither confirmed nor denied this, saying: "Not so fast, not so fast".

Chigir's meeting with parliamentary leaders, who are united against Lukashenko, suggested that he could be changing sides. This could deal a big blow to Lukashenko, who has launched an aggressive campaign to tighten his grip on rival institutions.

Lukashenko appointed Chigir prime minister after winning a landslide election in July 1994, wooing impoverished Belarussians with sensational promises to wipe out top-level corruption and rebuild a union with neighbouring Russia.
The prime minister is a well-respected figure in the republic of 10 million people.
Deputies have been occupying the chamber around the clock since Friday, fearing they could face the same fate as Viktor Gonchar, the man they named as Belarus's top electoral officer.
Gonchar was sacked by Lukashenko on Thursday and his security services barred him from his office and sealing off the Central Commission for Elections and Referendums.
Lukashenko kept up his campaign to muzzle the media late on Sunday, threatening through his Security Council to block broadcasts from neighbouring Russia's NTV television.
"NTV reported fights and bloodshed in Minsk. There was nothing of the kind. The republic's leadership will be forced to take appropriate steps," a Council statement said.
Lukashenko has threatened to deport Russian journalists caught without Belarussian accreditation and said he might extend the threat to foreign correspondents.
The former chief of a collective farm, Lukashenko sent postcards to the entire electorate at the weekend with a photograph of his smiling face and appeals to back him.

Every day state-run television advertisements urge people to take advantage of early voting if they cannot make it to the referendum on Sunday, when voters face a baffling list of questions posed by president and parliament.

The 42-year-old leader has attracted criticism abroad as well as at home for the referendum, in which he is seeking to extend his term by more than two years, appoint half the commission which monitors elections and half the constitutional court, and to name part of a new, upper house of parliament.
